Vince DiMartino

Vince DiMartino has led a distinguished career as a jazz educator and master of the trumpet. His teaching philosophy and his versatility in all genres of music have made him an invaluable contributor to the jazz and classical worlds.
Vince was interviewed via Zoom on January 8, 2025 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very pleased to have Vince DiMartino with me today. And we’re pretending you’re in Greece, is that correct?
Oh yeah. My mind is there a lot of times, every day.
Yeah. Well you’re a world traveler and you can’t see this because it’s in front of me but in the wall in front of me I have six pages of your resume.
Oh no.
On the right I have a page of handwritten notes, and on the left another page, and then I have these pages that I don’t have room for.
Terrible.
So my first question is how did you fit all this in?

Well first of all, I’m a teacher first. I’ve always wanted to be just like my high school band director, so I always made sure that I taught all my students every week and never missed any, because that was my primary goal, is to be an asset to that community no matter where I was teaching. It didn’t really matter if I was teaching junior high school students I would be the same. And then on the weekends, you know I would teach until Thursday afternoon and then I could get on a plane and I could fly to another university or some concert venue, you know, to play with some other folks: a brass quintet, jazz groups, a solo with wind ensembles, and stuff like that. And then I would come back on Sunday night.

There’s a lot to be said for that because I’m familiar with a number of people who are educators but they don’t have the same philosophy about that. They will reschedule lessons at the drop of a hat because they have a gig.

Right. Well you know to some degree I very rarely did anything longer than three or four days. It looks like I was gone forever you know, but I did an average of — I remember when I filled out my university forms you know every year they want to know what you’ve done. I usually had about — between my regional concerts and my other concerts, I had about 80 a year. So it looks like oh my God how did anybody do that. Well if it’s just like a local brass quintet gig it just says “and others” you know, but these were things that were actually formal concerts of some sort. And I did — about a third of them were © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

local, meaning in a hundred mile radius. And then some of them were — you know. And if I did have to leave more than four days I pre-taught my students before I left. I never wanted to be trying to play catch-up you know. That put me at ease both performing and teaching.

I think I know the answer to this question but do you feel it was a positive arrangement for you to be doing these concerts and these gigs and did it affect your teaching and what you could pass on to your students?

Oh yeah. Well you know it depended on what students. I taught mostly music ed students and applied students, some of which are pretty well known performers now. But they had needs and so I had to make sure that the syllabus — I used a very strict syllabus whereas most applied teachers don’t do that. You know you come into a lesson and everybody goes, “Oh that sounds better than last week.” But you know if you’re taking English class they give you a syllabus and there’s five books on there and you read those five books and you are responsible for the material, and then you get tested on it.
Did you create the syllabus?
Yeah. I’ll send it to you.
And did you create it — going back to this performing that you did in all aspects of music, did that find a place in the syllabus?

Yes in a sense. You know first of all a responsibility of a trumpet teacher, if you’re going to study with a trumpet teacher you have to learn how to play the trumpet. And a lot of students come to college and they have deficiencies. So the first two semesters of my syllabus are more or less expository. So everything is set up by keys and by like styles of music. Like I had one book that was called In the Singing Style. And what it was, was orchestra melodies, everything from a church hymn to a, you know, some kind of a part of some piece that a trumpet would play in an orchestra or something like that. So this way I could see, you know assess the depth of the knowledge of students in music. Then I would have the technical — we would start out with freshmen, everybody, it didn’t matter if they were virtuosic, all freshmen did the same course because you know what the academic ombudsman is, don’t you?
I’m going to let you tell me.

Well in most liberal arts colleges they usually don’t have one but I taught in Centres so I know that they don’t really have them. They have an academic counsel or something you know. But at State universities you know you have to treat everybody equally meaning from the standpoint of the coursework. You can’t say, “Oh, well Monk you know you’re not a very good reader so I’m going to give you this real easy thing to do and then at the end of the semester you can write a one-page summary of what we did this semester, and that’s all you need to do because you’re not as proficient” as this other person. Then this © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

other young person comes in, maybe the class is philosophy. “Well your mom and dad were both philosophers and they wrote books and things, so you have to read War and Peace and you have to tell me all the levels that this book is written on.” And then the guy that does the War and Peace gets a B, and guy that does the easy assignments because they just had no contact with music gets an A. You see that’s not fair. Just because that person is able you cannot treat them differently. So I wanted to make sure — and then also you find a lot of holes in that person that everybody thinks plays really well and that’s my job. My job is to bring everybody up to a certain standard. That’s what a course does. You have to learn as an applied teacher or any teacher in college you have to learn how to use their system to make what you need to happen happen. And over by you know like some people will turn in a syllabus that will say, “Fresh veneer, fundamentals.” What’s that? I mean that’s nothing. That’s say like, “Let’s eat.” You know what I mean? That’s fine but I mean I guess it’s effective but for that one situation — but I would say, “Let’s go to my favorite French restaurant. They have crepes. Crepes are this wonderful thing that you put stuff inside or on top of.” You see what I mean? You have to create depth if you are going to do something extraordinary.
Well in 1973 when you sort of started out was this philosophy in place?

Well no, it was — first of all I learned that the students couldn’t play the pieces that I knew. That was the first thing I learned. Well some of them. You know there were three or four that were good students, really. And they played the kind of literature that I knew. And the next person would come in you know I’ve never heard him play before and they obviously needed remedial work to play a moderately difficult piece, not even a difficult one. Even less than medium. So I started to really study literature. Because you know when you go to conservatory your teacher hands you the Haydn Trumpet Concerto or they hand you some other piece, the Tomasi Concerto where — “Oh you can play piccolo trumpet? Oh you’re going to play the Brandenburg Concerto” because they might be able to. But see like I said, you don’t find the shortcomings by only exposing a small part of what that student knows. Because it’s like students, when I used to practice when I first went to Eastman I didn’t want to sound bad in a practice room. All I ever played were things that I felt like I could — you know I tried to get those things better. And I knew I couldn’t play below the staff worth a darn so I didn’t really do that too much because you know, so that’s what you try to learn by setting up a syllabus. Because it’s very expository. You know it shows what the student can’t do. So even though they’re using the same syllabus, later, when I developed it a few years down the road, when I had my first sabbatical that was the very first thing I did. Because I was sort of doing it but it was still a little on the hodge-podge side you know. I had music ed students, so I had to figure out a way to use the same syllabus for music ed students. Like I said, “Well we’re going © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
to transpose.” “Well I don’t need to transpose.” I said, “Okay here’s this score, tell me what note the French horn is playing in concert pitch.” “Oh. Oh let’s see, that’s a” I’m going —
Time’s up.

That’s right. I’d say — the kids are way smarter than we are. I said, “If you can’t read the score they know it.” Because they know what their instruments can do and you don’t. Count lines you know. I said, “You can’t do that. You want to be an extraordinary band director. That means, it doesn’t mean you’re a genius. It means you’re out of the ordinary. There are no geniuses. There are extraordinary people. You know?
Okay I’m quoting — that’s quote number one today. I love it.

So I developed this — eventually I developed this syllabus. And the syllabus was to put everybody in the same course so that they had the same materials that they had to know as a graduating trumpet player or band director, and/or band director. You see what I mean? So that this way — now that said, the materials that you had to be tested on, and it’s in two-week modules — so the first week they come in and I say, “Well how did you do on the materials this week?” Because that’s the first week. See? Like so in other words you had two-week modules, the same material. That’s the only time you get to do that material. Then you get tested on it the second week. But if they’re a student, okay, that is fairly advanced. If they took private lessons they’re going to sail through the first stuff, except for maybe the things that they don’t do so well like, “You know your articulation is really not that good. You can play faster than lightening but you know but it’s not really clear what you’re doing.” So you can use them — especially if you use material that is familiar, very familiar to the teacher. You uncover those problems much easier, see? And then you can get right to the root of the problem on the same material. Now the next person I might say, “Well gee your lip slurs on that piece are, you know you really don’t have the right air, so let’s work on that to make sure that you have a tone line, that it doesn’t sound like” [scats]. I said, “Do you talk like that? Let’s go eat.” “Okay.” I said, “You don’t talk like that, do you?” I said, “I’m not making fun of you but” I said, “that’s what music is, people hear you and they have to understand what you’re saying. And the way they do that is through the evenness of your voice.” So we have to create that and so all these materials, and then at the same time those materials in the first two weeks are only in C and G. It was — because they were familiar with those keys. I want to put them at ease. I don’t want them to feel like you’re going to do C and C sharp today. These first two weeks. And they play C and they feel good and then they play C sharp and they can’t even play the scale. See? So I wanted to make sure it was progressive. You know it progressed to — they were learning discipline training, because they only had two weeks to learn the materials. Then they went away and they had the next two weeks, F and D. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

See what I mean? So you’re adding accidentals and you’re adding the appropriate etudes that are in those keys. So they’re playing like in that key for two weeks. They don’t have other keys. And then they have to learn it. So the reason, once again, is to put everybody on an even keel. When you go to English class and you’re the worst reader in the class it takes you longer to read the books. It takes you longer to understand reading faster what’s going on. It takes you longer to understand the plot or whatever, whatever your weakness is. But hopefully the materials, if they’re chosen right by the teacher, will allow you to start figuring out what needs the most work. Of course you go to lessons and that’s really what we talk about.
I’m going to leapfrog to after you’ve had these students for years perhaps —
Yeah, four years.
Okay. Have you ever had students who get to the point who can play things that you can’t?
Not really.
Okay.

Not really, and that’s because I mean I don’t expect all my colleagues to do what I’ve done, which is my own passion for playing. I mean I — people would say to me, “Why are you in Kentucky?” I’d say, “Well why are you anywhere?” I said because you can be an asset to that community. When I stepped foot in Kentucky and started that it was a one-year appointment. And I knew after the first month that I didn’t want to leave because there was activity in the trumpet there but it was not anything extraordinary. And so now I think the thing I feel the best about, besides the students that are teaching at other universities and playing in service bands and professional groups and things, other orchestras, I think my greatest achievement is having enriched the community in which I live. What could be better? You know I found out my neighbor, he plays all over the world. You know after you’ve lived there for twenty years. Because he’d never played there. You know he’d go out on these trips and traveling, and then you play one recital a year at the university you know and that’s it. And then nobody comes to that most of the time except other faculty and friends. So basically like I started a duo there because when I got there there was nothing for me to play in in Kentucky. It was 110,000 people in Lexington and now there’s almost 400,000. So I said well I’ve got to do something here so I’m going to volunteer to play with high school bands. I just visited in Florida here with the band director of the first concert I did with a high school band in Kentucky. Excellent band. And he asked me, and his son played trumpet. So I gave his son trumpet lessons and you know I played with him at the Midwest Band Clinic. I played with all the best bands in Kentucky at the Midwest Band Clinic. And to me that was the greatest thing. And today I have students all over not only of course other places but Kentucky, © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

that teach in schools, that are excellent teachers. I have students that teach other young people about trumpet. I have students — all the students in my big band they were students at U.K. See? And they wouldn’t be in there if they couldn’t play it. Because they know me better, and it’s like my son, right? You know he’s a great trumpet player. He taught at — I think it was Colgate, I’m not sure.
Syracuse I think he was at.

He was at Syracuse but he played in an orchestra that was either in Hamilton or Colgate, I can’t remember. Because I went there but I wasn’t there in the day I was there at night just to hear his rehearsal.
I see.
I did go to Colgate when I was in high school though. I went to American Legion Boys State.
All right.
And I played a solo with the band at the All-State. You know you got appointed by your local county. I don’t even remember. But I loved it up there. All I remember was you had to walk up this hill.
Yes, lots of hills at Colgate.

And it was hot. And I was trying to figure out how I could only walk up the hill once, you know, because it was so hot there. You know and I’m from New York, from Long Island you know so we knew what the summers were like but not like that when you were walking up that hill. We didn’t have those hills on Long Island.
Well I want to ask you, as a kid I had a couple of moments that really put me on a path, it was fortunate. And I read this anecdote about you had a semester away and you were in Bogota, Colombia.
That’s right.
I’d love to hear the details about this story.

It’s a good story because it really relates to my life choices. And that is, when I was in high school, you know I was a good student. And so you know that’s how I got to go to Bogota, the school sent me for free. And they sent another girl who was one of my good friends, she went to Guatemala. And I was sent to Colombia. They chose two students and for different reasons. I wasn’t the highest academic in the school, but I was up in the classes with those people. And so I went. I was getting ready — my dentist, who lived on the wealthy side of the street, the big street, you know he was a dentist. And his daughter was one of my best friends. We consulted on our homework at night you know. “Oh man, that trigonometry, that question number six did you —” you know and that kind of thing. “Did you get the answer to that? I kept getting this X — that ain’t it, you know what I mean?” And then we’d talk and I say, “Oh jeez, I missed that stupid decimal point, oh my © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

gosh.” But her dad was a dentist, okay? And you know I told him and I said, “Well you know I want to be either a doctor or a dentist.” You know I figured I want to live on that side of the street, that’s a pretty good place to be. So he said, “Well you can come over, and come to the office and you know see what I do.” So I went like once a week or once every two weeks, and I sterilized his stuff. Now they just throw it away and use new ones. But you know he had a sterilization thing and you put all the used instruments in there and then he can use them for the next patient or the next day or whatever. And he also gave me a nice white coat that I could watch what he was doing. And I wasn’t really excited you know about the stuff lying around in people’s mouth and everything. But I said well I can do this. I can probably do this. And I said well maybe I’ll go to a medical school and be a doctor. And I said well that’s not going to be any easier you know. So that was my junior year, and I went between my junior and senior year. And so I went down to Colombia. And it was about — I forget what the name of it — it was called the Open Door Exchange Program. And so you know there were about I don’t know, twelve, a dozen other students from different places on Long Island you know that went to the same place. And we had meetings and they took us on excursions. We went to Cartagena from Bogota and stayed about like two or three days and saw all the beautiful things there on the coast. But the family I was staying with, they had a sort of a — almost like a small cottage in the lowlands. Because Bogota is like about 7,000 feet up in the mountains. It’s about like Denver or something. And it rained there every day for about ten minutes and then it was absolutely gorgeous the rest of the time. And it was that way all year long. So they would take us down to the coast and they were kind of wealthy. There was a little country club there. And the place we stayed in was rustic at best. Spartan. I used to call it the “Spartan Arms” because you slept in a hammock in some of the rooms, and they had a swimming pool. The only thing that was there was they had their own swimming pool and they had this block, cement block cottage thing. And you could fit about five people in there and some of them sleeping in the living room. But the country club was great food and they had like traditional dancing there. So it was kind of neat. So after I’d been there a month man I wasn’t playing with anybody. I wasn’t doing anything. So there was a dance at this big hotel, the Hotel Tequendama. And it was a, you know at the time it was like “the” hotel so if your school had a dance they did it there because it was their big deal. And so I went and they had this cumbia band that played that music and I said, wow that’s really interesting stuff. I heard that on the radio and I said now I’m watching the musicians do this. And I told them I said, “Well I play trumpet you know.” So they said, “Well you can come back.” I said, “Well yeah, I played in the like All-State groups and stuff like that in America.” He says, “Well you can come back if you want to try to play with us.” So I did, I went back the next week and I played with them and they said, © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

“Oh boy you sound great.” And I said, “Well,” I said, “I’d like to play somewhere.” And they said, “Well there’s a place, it’s not in the best section of Bogota but it’s called ‘Freddie’s American Jazz Bar’ and they have a trio there that you might like to listen to at least.” And I said, “Well that’s great.” So I found my way over there, and I didn’t, you know this was great because you know the families you were staying with, they didn’t want you going to like, almost like going to Harlem or something. You know what I mean? They didn’t want you going there. They had glass in their wall around their house because you know crime is a big thing. They didn’t have a regular police force there. Military police. They carry machine guns. You know they walk around the city, you see these guys with machine guns you know. At night you hear [scats]. Sometimes you know I’m going I’m glad my mom and dad didn’t know about this you know what I mean because I didn’t know either. So anyway so I found this place and I went over there. Same kind of thing. They said, “Well you could bring your trumpet and we’d see what you do.” And I played a couple of tunes with them and they said, “Can you come back every week?” I said, “Well you know I have a lot of friends and we only can get together, I can only go out at night when I go out with my friends.” So if you will feed my friends — and you know it was a bar like, you know it was like a nice place but it was a bar. And he said, “Well we usually don’t have a lot of young people in here.” And I was about 18, 17. And I said, “Well can’t you make a place where they just sit?” “Okay.” And every time we’d come, almost every week and I’d come there and the table would be filled with food and I’d play and all my exchange student friends were there and they loved it and the people started coming you know. And so I said, “You know I really like doing this. This is what I really like to do” I said. And putting the thing in somebody’s mouth and seeing blood fly around with pieces of their teeth, that just really, I don’t think — what’s the choice here you know? So I had already, when I went back I talked to my mom first, I said, “Mom you know I don’t think I want to be a doctor.” And she said, “Well that’s all right.” I said, “Really?” She said, “Well you know look at you’re a really good student, look at what you’ve done on trumpet, look what you’ve done in school, why would I be worried about what you’re going to do? You’re going to do well.” You know and she was great. I said, “Wow, thanks for that, Mom, you can tell dad.” You know it was really funny. And my mom was really the center of our whole family, even the grandparents and everything. Because she had the joie de vivre. And when she said, “Oh come on we have to get together on Sunday, come on out from the city (my grandparents).”
What was that descriptor you just used for her?
Joie de vivre?
Yeah.
Joy for life. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
Okay. You must have not been a person who was afraid to take a chance, to basically improvise?

No. I didn’t learn by reading music. Because even though I started in the public schools you know that was sort of fundamentally [scats] and but my neighbor was a bass player. My back neighbor where I would climb over the fence and he had a little jazz group that he would rehearse. He was like an engineer at Sperry Gyroscope out on Long Island. He played bass. Genius. He was telling me about how they were working on the gyroscopes that would send the rockets up and stuff. I mean he was great. But my dad said to him, my dad was a tap dancer during the war, overseas. I mean he did everything from being a cook to a tank driver, and he would entertain tap dancing when they were doing some sort of event to keep everybody upbeat. You know? And so what was I saying — so he asked the bass player, in the back, he said, “Hey Bob, you know my son’s been playing trumpet and I think he sounds pretty good, so is there any recordings that I should have, I should get him?” And we didn’t have a lot of money. So he named like four recordings and it was Miles Davis, Maynard Ferguson, Rafael Mendez and Billy Butterfield.
Oh, nice mix.

Yep. That’s why I think he, this guy was like I say, he was really organized in his thoughts and his work. So I had these four records, you know the LPs and a changer. And every day after school that’s what I did. I practiced. I did my homework first, always. My schoolwork. And so then I did my trumpet until dinner. I did my homework while my mom was cooking I did it in the kitchen at the table. And she was cooking and I said [sniffs] “Oh what is that, Mom? That smells really good.” And that’s how I learned to cook. I never cooked for many years except by smell when I finally started to cook a lot I just remembered what it smelled like. I said, “I think this is close.” And then, “I think that was too much garlic maybe.” So I would practice with these records at least an hour a day.
Can you define what you were — how were you practicing? Were you copying?
Yes.
You were trying to get what these trumpet players were playing?

Yes and I thought that I was like the worst trumpet player that ever lived, because I couldn’t play a lot of the stuff that was on the records. Try to play along with Maynard Ferguson and I’m going, “They don’t even have the fingerings in the book for this, so how am I supposed to do this?” You know. So I said, “Well I’ll just use the ones an octave lower.” And then it worked and you know so, and I played in band, in middle school band and when I finally — I remember when I was in middle school band that we were reading like a simple march book, the Bennett Band Book I remember it was a little, you know one of these things. And they had like easy versions of marches. And they © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

started playing and I said what? How come there’s three eighth notes in a beat? I don’t get this. Because it was 6/8 you see. And I didn’t understand how 6/8 worked and — I could play it, because once I heard somebody play it I figured it out you know. But I really was, I mean I always practiced. When I was in junior high school I practiced at least a couple of hours a day. At least. And I listened. See? And I always tell people today, no matter what lessons they’re taking, I say, “Practicing is a good thing.” I said, “If you only like to practice a half hour a day and you just want to learn to play a little bit and play in a group then you only have to listen a half hour a day.” I said, “If you want to practice more than that then you have to practice the equivalent time listening. Otherwise you have no vocabulary. All you have is words. You have just words and they don’t make any sense to anybody.” See you know and the inflection, I said, “You have to learn the vernacular language of whatever is on the recording.” If I’m listening to a classical symphony — which I did — I worked at Lockheed where my dad worked, Lockheed Aircraft at Kennedy Airport when it was there, before they moved. And I was the receiving clerk one summer. And I had one of those — you know those radios that have the antenna was the handle?
Oh yes.

Well that’s what I had. And it was green and it had that patent leather all over it. And I used to listen to WPAT, New Jersey, which was right over the river from the airport. And it was all classical. Because by that time I was going to go to Eastman. I was in Eastman at the time. And these guys, they had to come and they had runners for parts you know. And they would come and say, “I want this part here, number 4 —” I said, “Wait,” I said, “what is that music you’re listening to? I said, “That’s the music you’re going to have to listen to before I get your part.” You know cement heads I was working with. But I understood. I understood all that. But I listened all the time. Because when I found music, and I tell students the same thing. I said — I listen to rock & roll. And the reason I did was because well I was a kid and we all listened to rock & roll. And I said, you know these chords that they’re playing, some notes stay the same and some notes change. And most of the time they don’t change much. So I was learning theory right away. See? And I learned to play with those ideas in my mind. So well that note stays the same almost the whole time. I can work off of that note you know what I mean? I was clueless, you know?

Sort of anticipated a question I had about that and that was especially in the rock & roll or the jazz is playing the trumpet parts, or playing along with it, was there a point where you got a sense of also hearing the bass notes and figuring out okay this is in mostly this key that’s why these trumpet parts sort of make sense? © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Yeah. My first job was when I was 14. Okay? With older musicians. Because I lived about 400 yards from an American Legion — no it wasn’t an American Legion — it was like one of those little party houses. Not a big one, just a little one. And they would have weddings in there and you know the Italian club would meet there and you know things like that. So one night about 9:00 the phone rings and some guy is talking to my dad and he goes, “Absolutely not.” I’m going what’s going on, what’s going on? He says, “No, my son’s not coming out at 9:00 and play with your band. I know you heard he plays pretty well but well okay, I’m coming over there with him.” So he took me over to this place and you know what? My neighbor had given me a fake book. See I did that after school too. I learned some tunes. I didn’t really know the chord changes at all really. So the very first thing I heard from the band leader, “Oh thanks for coming. ‘Perdido’ in B flat.” That was all I had.
Did you have a B flat fake book?
No, no I had a C.
So you had a concert fake book, did you read?
I transposed it. So then I had to play off the staff. And my band director of course in high school, okay, he was great.
We should get his name on the record.
His name? Edward DeUlio.
Ilio?

DeUlio. Large D, small E, Large I — L-I-O. U-I-L-O. DeUlio. And I mean I think of him almost every day, still. Because he was just remarkable, a remarkable person you know. And he would say — anytime I had time I was in the band room practicing. During lunch I would eat lunch in 10 minutes and I’d go over to the band room and practice. And that’s just what I did. Not some esoteric music trumpet guru type of stuff. Otherwise who understands that? That’s not their vernacular. You know? So for me that was always the most important thing. And so when they came to school, even if, you know, one of my students said something I’ll never forget. He was a freshman, okay? And he was playing his jury, you know his jury exam. Every semester that you take applied lessons you have to play for the class faculty and then they give you comments and they try to help you and, you know, that’s great. So and what I used to do, especially with the freshmen that I knew were nervous playing their first, you know, jury. And they’re standing up on a stage and people are looking at them. They’ve never played a recital. Well usually they’ve © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

played one because everybody gets on stage once at a big recital that everybody plays on, and plays all or part of a movement of a piece and only with the trumpet players there as their audience. So anyway they’ve been on stage. But in the meantime they haven’t been in this situation where they’re getting graded for it, you know, and stuff. So I get off stage and I said, “Well, John, what are you going to play?” And he goes, “I’m going to play that there Heyden song.” And I realized where I was, you know what I mean? He never said that in, because I never asked him that question you know. And I felt bad because you know the faculty, one of them laughed you know what I mean? And I just — oh gosh this is awful. I said, this isn’t going to happen to anybody. I have to teach people, you know, how to — and I never said, “Haydn song” in lessons. You know but every time a student mispronounced a word, I said, “Oh no, that’s not Heyden” it’s Haydn. I said, “I used to say Heyden.” But you’re going to say Haydn.
Yeah. Make them feel okay about it, yeah.

After that, after than, and you know when I do master classes it’s the same thing. I’ll go in and I’ll say, “You want to sound like that? This is what you do to fix that.” And they try it and they go, “That’s pretty good.” Well how did I know how to fix that? That’s what I used to do. I said, “All the things that you all are doing,” I said, “I used to do.” So don’t think that I’m some sort of a savant or something. I said, “I just spent an extraordinary amount of time wasted trying to figure out how to do it right.” And I said, “And I’m glad I did it, because I don’t want you to do that. I want to be a catalytic person in your life. I want you to skip all the bad things that I did to try to learn how to play the trumpet.” I said, like for instance, like the book that I wrote, it’s not a book, it’s just a manual for the students to read about how the trumpet works and stuff like that. But I don’t want, most of the books that I’ve ever gotten/bought, I have every book known to man. Like I said, I have 15,000 entries in my library at home. So I’ve got a lot of books and pieces. I said, “You know most of them don’t have much writing in them at all, they just, you know like play these magic etudes and you’ll be better.” No. You’ll be better at playing the way you play and hopefully getting half the notes and still sounding bad. So I said, so the book that I wrote, everything in that book, if you play it wrong it sounds bad. It’s just going to sound bad. From the beginning to the end, it’s one technique. But nobody knows that. They’re just trying to learn all these new materials and I’m working on the same thing every lesson using the materials to fine tune what I should be talking to them about. Because once again, the materials are remedial to start and then after we get along I can even give them more stuff, they get less entries in the lesson thing that are longer, but they’re longer. See? So you start out with short things they can do. [scats] You know Arban ’93. Yeah. So the old ’93. So they learn the whole thing by the end of the semester rather than say okay I want you to learn all of page 93. They can’t play in half of those keys. They’re going to just hate trumpet, they’re going to hate taking lessons. And if they practice, they won’t because they catch up to the ones that don’t practice that are already can play those things. They think they can.

He says, “I might someday get close to that.” Right. And I said, “Steve,” I said, “this is just like trumpet playing.” I said, “It’s great. segments.title: Opening and Monk Rowe's introduction
segments.summary: Boilerplate, then Rowe introduces Vince DiMartino on Zoom and remarks on his enormous resume.

segments.title: Teacher first: fitting 80 concerts a year around teaching
segments.summary: DiMartino says teaching came first; he taught all week and flew out for concerts, pre-teaching students if away over four days.

segments.title: Does performing help teaching; the strict syllabus
segments.summary: He says his strict trumpet syllabus served music ed and applied students, like an English class syllabus, and he offers to send it.

segments.title: Designing the syllabus: expository materials and fairness
segments.summary: The first semesters assess students with orchestra melodies and keyed material; everyone gets the same course so no one is treated differently.

segments.title: Starting at Kentucky in 1973: students who could not play the literature
segments.summary: In 1973 he found students needed remedial work, so he studied literature and built a syllabus, even making music ed students read scores.

segments.title: Two-week modules and progressive keys
segments.summary: The syllabus runs in two-week modules by key, starting with C and G, building discipline and evenness of tone.

segments.title: Enriching the Kentucky community
segments.summary: He has not been outplayed by students; his greatest achievement is enriching Lexington through high school bands, a duo and former students.

segments.title: His son and Colgate Boys State memories
segments.summary: A tangent about his son's teaching and his own visit to Colgate for American Legion Boys State in high school.

segments.title: Bogota exchange semester and the dentist's office
segments.summary: Sent to Colombia for free as a student, after shadowing a dentist, he sat in with a cumbia band at a hotel dance.

segments.title: Freddie's jazz bar and deciding against medicine
segments.summary: He played at Freddie's American Jazz Bar with his exchange friends fed, then told his mother he would not be a doctor.

segments.title: Neighbor bassist and the four records
segments.summary: Learning by ear, he got four records on a neighbor's advice: Miles Davis, Ferguson, Mendez and Butterfield, and his mother's cooking.

segments.title: Copying records, practicing and listening
segments.summary: He copied the records daily, learned theory from rock & roll, and advises equal listening and practice time.

segments.title: First job at 14: 'Perdido' in B flat
segments.summary: At 14 he was called to a local party house band, handed 'Perdido' in B flat, and transposed from a C fake book.

segments.title: Band director Edward DeUlio and buying records
segments.summary: His high school band director's rotating lessons, Glenn Drewes, and his paper route money spent on records.

segments.title: Soloing on 'Perdido' and the $18 pay
segments.summary: He faked the solo from the melody's outline, played with that band for years, and was paid about $18.

segments.title: Being an asset to your community
segments.summary: He tells students to be an asset to any community, from Carnegie Hall to funerals, and dislikes wedding coordinators.

segments.title: Playing is acting: same person, different costume
segments.summary: Asked about Stravinsky versus Clark Terry's band, he says playing is acting, honoring each composer, even in rock groups.

segments.title: Music is something you do between meals
segments.summary: He puts family first, calls music something done between meals, and explains why he studied orchestral trumpet.

segments.title: Arriving at Eastman as a self-taught outsider
segments.summary: At Eastman without a jazz program he was a back-door learner, and found local Rochester orchestra attitudes unappealing.

segments.title: Recitals, brass quintet, and playing behind Aretha Franklin
segments.summary: He talks of trumpet and organ recitals, concentration in brass quintet, and listening during rests behind Aretha Franklin.

segments.title: Music is sound not sight: solfeggio, conductors and the Hindemith Sonata
segments.summary: He argues notation is a shortcut, criticizes conductors who only teach rehearsing, and describes learning phrasing from string bowings.

segments.title: West Babylon band and the director's silent looks
segments.summary: He describes his small, inclusive high school band and how his director looked at him to signal mistakes.

segments.title: Worst gigs: 50 Acres and Pilgrim State Hospital
segments.summary: Asked about bizarre gigs, he tells of a depressing job with elderly players in Rochester and playing a veterans' show at Pilgrim State.

segments.title: Playing 'Portrait of George' at Carnegie Hall in a janitor's closet
segments.summary: With the Cincinnati Pops and Erich Kunzel, he had to play off stage and ended up in a janitor's closet, which relieved his nerves.

segments.title: First big recital with the organist and lack of confidence at Eastman
segments.summary: A recital with organist Schuyler drew 500 people; he recalls lacking confidence at Eastman despite his seats.

segments.title: Rowe praises DiMartino, with Milt Hinton, Joe Wilder and Clark Terry
segments.summary: Rowe says people light up at his name, as with Hinton, Wilder and Terry, and thanks him.

segments.title: Writing for Viper, Kentucky and the 'Heyden' jury
segments.summary: He wrote his manual for a trumpeter in Viper, Kentucky, and tells of a freshman mispronouncing Haydn at a jury.

segments.title: Master classes and the manual using Arban
segments.summary: He says he wants to spare students his wasted effort, and explains his manual and Arban page 93 keyed by the week.

segments.title: Practicing technique and music together: Baroque recital and the racing engine
segments.summary: He describes practicing before the call, the Bonneville engine analogy, and demonstrates phrasing over mechanics.

segments.title: Friendly chat and Greg Caputo, Joe Wilder
segments.summary: The two enjoy each other, talk of meeting in person and a shared connection to Greg Caputo and Joe Wilder.

segments.title: Clark Terry, Cadillac Williams and Richard Williams
segments.summary: Clark Terry named Joe Wilder, Snooky and Cadillac Williams; DiMartino recalls playing a solo after Terry on video.

segments.title: Playing with Lionel Hampton at 19, and Wallace Davenport
segments.summary: At about 19 he played in Hampton's big band and small group alongside Wallace Davenport, a circular-breathing trumpeter who studied French.

segments.title: The end of an era and training students for gigs
segments.summary: He says he was at the end of an era of working bands, and in Lexington took students on gigs and trained them.

segments.title: Roland Kirk at The Fishnet
segments.summary: He brought his big band to open for Roland Kirk at The Fishnet and was amazed by his multiple saxophones.

segments.title: Rochester jazz: Bill Evans and the Pythod
segments.summary: He saw Bill Evans every year in Rochester and recalls the Pythod and drummer Vinnie.

segments.title: Arrangers Holiday and the summer trumpet section
segments.summary: At Eastman's Arrangers Holiday he sight-read and recorded, leading a section of Mosello, Tyzik and Vizutti.

segments.title: Refusing first trumpet and winning the lead trumpet pay raise
